job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems

This analysis covers the manager's amendment text as you pasted it. Issues are grouped by section, and the most consequential are flagged **[Major]**.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A) [Major]:** The 10,000-ton threshold applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could spread recovery across several vessels, each staying under the cap. Nothing aggregates tonnage across vessels, affiliates, or a common operator.

2. **§2(1)(A):** The bill doesn't say whether "metric tons" means wet or dry weight. Freshly recovered nodules hold a large share of water, so the choice can significantly change whether an operation crosses the threshold.

3. **§2(1)(A):** "Per year" is undefined. Calendar year, fiscal year, and rolling 12 months each give different results, and swapping vessels mid-year could reset the count.

4. **§2(1)(A):** "Recovery" is undefined. It's unclear whether it means collection on the seabed, lifting to the surface, or landing ashore, and whether a collector vehicle or riser system counts as part of "the vessel" or as separate equipment.

5. **§2(1)(A):** "Other mineral resources" is undefined. It could arguably reach sand, gravel, or hydrocarbons, which invites both overbreadth challenges and narrowing interpretations.

6. **§2(1)(A) [Major]:** The definition has no geographic scope. It doesn't say whether it covers the U.S. EEZ and continental shelf, areas beyond national jurisdiction, or both. It also doesn't explain how it relates to existing regimes such as the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) and the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA).

7. **§2(1)(B) [Major]:** "The Secretary" is never defined (Commerce? Interior?), so it's unclear who holds this authority.

8. **§2(1)(B) [Major]:** The provision gives an open-ended power to designate new prohibited activities, with no standards, procedures, or rulemaking requirement. Because §5(b) attaches criminal penalties to these determinations, the provision is exposed to void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges. After *Loper Bright*, the agency also gets no deference on how it reads "comparable" risks.

9. **§2(2) [Major]:** "U.S. person" covers only citizens and corporations "organized under the laws of a State." That leaves out:
   - lawful permanent residents;
   - entities organized under D.C., territorial, or federal law;
   - arguably LLCs and partnerships, which are not "corporations";
   - foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies.

   A U.S. parent could therefore run operations through a foreign-incorporated affiliate operating outside the United States.

10. **§2(3):** "Covered vessel" is used only in the §4 registry, not in the prohibition. The 5,000-gross-ton floor exempts smaller vessels from registration. "Equipped for" recovery could be avoided by using modular equipment that is installed only when needed.

11. **§2 generally:** The bill doesn't define "person," "United States," "seabed," "Secretary," "exploration license," or "environmental assessment." Each term is a likely point of dispute.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

12. **§3(a):** "In the United States" has no geographic definition, so it's unclear whether it reaches the EEZ or U.S.-flagged vessels on the high seas. A foreign person aboard a U.S.-flagged vessel beyond U.S. waters may fall outside the ban.

13. **§3(a) [Major]:** The bill prohibits only "engag[ing] in" mining. It does not prohibit financing, sponsoring, chartering, processing, or importing minerals recovered by others. It also has no civil aiding-and-abetting provision; 18 U.S.C. §2 covers only the criminal side.

14. **§3(b) [Major]:** The grandfather clause has several gaps:
    - It has no expiration date.
    - It doesn't address renewals, extensions, transfers, or amendments, so a pre-enactment license could arguably be renewed indefinitely or sold.
    - "Exploration license" isn't limited to licenses issued by U.S. authorities, so it could arguably cover foreign or International Seabed Authority instruments.

15. **§3(b):** The clause exempts "mining" under an *exploration* license. Exploration licenses don't authorize commercial recovery, so it's unclear whether the clause is meant to (and does) shelter commercial-scale recovery. A court could read it either way.

16. **§3(b):** The cutoff is "date of enactment," not introduction or a fixed date. That gives an incentive to obtain licenses between now and enactment, and the bill says nothing about applications pending on that date.

17. **§3(c) [Major]:** The environmental-assessment exemption is defined only by purpose. It has no tonnage cap, permit requirement, agency approval, or definition of "environmental assessment," and doesn't say whether that purpose must be the sole or primary one. Any operation could claim it, and the government would bear the burden of disproving the stated purpose.

## Sec. 4: Registry

18. **§4 [Major]:** The registry has no enforcement mechanism. §5's penalties apply only to violations of §3, so failing to register or report carries no penalty under this Act (aside from possible 18 U.S.C. §1001 liability for false statements).

19. **§4(a):** The section sets no deadline for registration and doesn't say whether foreign operators or foreign-flagged vessels must register.

20. **§4(b):** The reporting requirement is weak:
    - Reports are self-certified, with no required content (such as tonnage, location, or depth).
    - NOAA has no verification, inspection, or monitoring authority.
    - Reports are not made public.

    As a result, the registry can't reliably detect violations of the tonnage threshold.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

21. **§5(a) vs. §8 [Major]:** §5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 makes the Act effective 180 days *after* enactment. Activity during that window is in legal limbo and could support due process or fair-notice challenges.

22. **§5(a):** The threshold is measured per year, but penalties are assessed per day. It's unclear which "day" a violation occurs on: the day the threshold is crossed, every day of the year, or each day afterward.

23. **§5(a):** The bill doesn't say who assesses civil penalties, through what process (administrative or judicial), or what notice and hearing rights apply. No enforcement agency is designated anywhere in the Act.

24. **§5(a):** A penalty of up to $1 million per day, with no mitigating factors, invites an Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines challenge in individual cases.

25. **§5 generally:** The bill provides no injunctive relief, forfeiture of vessels or recovered minerals, investigative or subpoena powers, boarding authority, or citizen-suit provision. Enforcement tools are thin, especially for operations offshore.

26. **§5(b):** Criminal liability is tied to §3, which includes Secretary-designated activities under §2(1)(B). That compounds the vagueness problem in item 8 and raises the bar for proving willfulness.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

27. **§6:** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" is ambiguous. It could mean negotiations must *begin* within 18 months or be *concluded* by then. Either way, the duty is hortatory, has no reporting requirement, and has no consequence if no agreement results.

## Sec. 7: Duration

28. **§7(a) vs. §7(b) [Major]:** The two subsections conflict. (a) says the ban lasts "until" Congress acts by joint resolution, while (b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. Because the sunset runs from enactment but the Act takes effect 180 days later, the ban effectively lasts about 9.5 years.

29. **§7(a):** The provision doesn't direct NASEM to produce a report, provide funding, or set a timeline, and "serious harm" is undefined. It's also legally superfluous, because Congress can always repeal the Act by ordinary legislation.

30. **§7(b):** There is no savings clause. It's unclear whether penalties for violations that occurred before the sunset can still be enforced after it. The general savings statute, 1 U.S.C. §109, may apply, but its application to expiring statutes is litigable.

## Cross-Cutting Issues

31. **Relationship to existing law [Major]:** The bill doesn't amend or repeal DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.) or address OCSLA. NOAA's authority to issue commercial recovery permits would remain on the books, creating a direct statutory conflict that courts would have to resolve.

32. **No rulemaking authority:** No agency is authorized to issue regulations implementing §§2 to 5. That makes it hard to fill the definitional gaps above without risking challenges that the agency exceeded its authority.

33. **No severability clause:** Courts generally presume severability, but if §2(1)(B) or §3(b) were struck down, the lack of a clause invites argument over whether the rest of the Act survives.

---

**A note for markup prep:** Bill sponsors and committee staff will likely spot many of these issues, especially items 1, 9, 17, 18, 21, and 28. Expect technical amendments addressing them on Thursday. It may help to prepare positions on likely fixes (vessel aggregation, a tighter grandfather clause, a defined assessment permit), not only the current text. Please have counsel confirm the legal points (*Loper Bright*, 1 U.S.C. §109, Excessive Fines) before relying on them in any external materials.
